question.:question/problem: Find the slope of the normal line to the curve $y=- 28 x^{\frac{5}{2}} + 7 x^{3}$ at the point $(1,-21).$
question.:question/worked-solution:
Let $f(x)=- 28 x^{\frac{5}{2}} + 7 x^{3}.$ Computing the derivative $f'(1)$ gives

$$
\begin{aligned}f'(x) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(- 28 x^{\frac{5}{2}} + 7 x^{3}) \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(-28{x}^{\frac{5}{2}}+7{x}^{3}) \\  & =-70{x}^{\frac{3}{2}}+21{x}^{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

We then compute $f'(1)$, which gives

$$
\begin{aligned}m=f'(1) & =-70\cdot (1)^{\frac{3}{2}}+21\cdot (1)^{2}=-49.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the slope of the normal line  ${m}^{′}$ is

$$
m'=-\frac{1}{m}=\frac{1}{49}.
$$

question.:question/worked-solution:
Let $f(x)=\frac{5 x^{5}}{2} - 40 x^{2}.$ First, we compute the derivative:

$$
f'(x)=\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\frac{5 x^{5}}{2} - 40 x^{2})=\frac{25 x^{4}}{2} - 80 x
$$

Then, we compute the slope of the tangent at the point $(2,-80):$

$$
m=f'(2)=\frac{25}{2}\cdot (2)^{4}-80\cdot (2)=200-160=40
$$

Therefore, the slope ${m}^{'}$ of the normal line is

$$
\begin{aligned}m' & =-\frac{1}{m} \\  & =-\frac{1}{(40)} \\  & =- \frac{1}{40}.\end{aligned}
$$
